issues.issue: The effective date is left blank ("effective as of ____________"), yet Section 2.15 defines "Effective Date" as "the date first stated above" and dozens of deadlines run from it. The date the Agreement takes effect therefore cannot be fixed from the instrument's own words.

The recital fixes the project only in approximations ("approximately 124 communities", "approximately 1,392 community anchor institutions"), and those approximations feed the 90%-of-CAIs test in the Commencement Date definition. What counts as the denominator is not stated.

This recital that Network Operator "is experienced and skilled" could be argued to operate as a warranty of capability alongside the express warranties in Section 5.1.6 and 5.1.7. A court could be asked whether a recital creates obligations beyond Article 5.

The recital describes the services "among other things," an open-ended catch-all that sits against the specific enumeration of duties in Article 4 and the definition of "Services" in Section 2.60. A party could argue the recital enlarges the operative scope of work.

"Functions, responsibilities and tasks ... otherwise commonly performed by a dark fiber and lit network provider" imports unwritten industry duties with no stated benchmark. The phrase is vague and could be used to expand the Services beyond what Article 4 lists.

The rule that "all capitalized terms shall have the meanings set forth in this Article 2" fails when read against the rest of the instrument, which uses capitalized terms Article 2 never defines (e.g. "Attachment Database" in 4.3.4, "CAPEX Upgrade and Update Fund" in 4.9.6, "Termination Date" in 3.6.1.1, "Initial Plan" in 4.1.10.1, "Applicable Third Party" in 7.3.2). The definitional rule cannot be given effect as written.

This fixes the AAA Rules "in effect at the time a demand for arbitration is made," whereas the Guaranty Agreement's Section 4.6 elects AAA Commercial Rules "in effect on the date of the Agreement" and contemplates consolidation of the two proceedings. Which rule set governs a consolidated arbitration is unresolved.

"Control" is used three times to define Affiliate but is itself left undefined and carries no percentage or other threshold, unlike the 50% voting-securities test Section 8.1.4 supplies for change of control. The reach of "Affiliate" in Sections 4.8, 2.45 and 9.1 is therefore uncertain.

The definition points to "Section 4.9.2" for the Annual Plan, but Section 4.9.2 concerns agreements between MTC and third parties; the Annual Plan is actually required by Section 4.9.3.2. The cross-reference is wrong on its face.

MTC may revise the Exhibit A list of CAIs "in MTC's sole discretion up until the Commencement Date," while Section 2.8(a) makes the Commencement Date turn on 90% of "the CAIs" being connected. MTC can thus move the very target that determines when its own trigger is met.

Because the Commencement Date is "the earlier of" the 90% completion test or thirty months after the Effective Date, it arrives at thirty months even if the network is largely unbuilt, which is squarely the situation Section 4.9.2.8 addresses by merely reducing payments. Whether Network Operator's Commencement-Date obligations (e.g. the CAPEX payments under 4.9.6) nonetheless begin is left in doubt.

Confidential Information turns on what "would reasonably be understood by the Parties, to be proprietary or confidential," a standard with no boundary, and is expressly made subject to the Public Records Act. What is actually protected is indeterminate.

A Dark Fiber Customer is defined as a lessee "from MTC pursuant to Section 4.7.4," yet Section 4.7.4.4 contemplates a Dark Fiber Customer leasing from the Network Operator in its own name on a Network Operator Network Extension. The two cannot both be squared with the definition.
"The date first stated above" refers to the preamble, where the date is left blank. The Effective Date, from which nearly every deadline in Article 4 runs, cannot be determined from the document.

"Any financial statements of Network Operator delivered to MTC" defines the term by the act of delivery rather than by content, so it captures whatever is handed over. Its interaction with the specific statements required by Section 4.9.9 is unclear.

"Strikes" appear both in the unqualified enumerated list and again in the closing qualifier limiting them to strikes "not resulting from the responsible Party's ... failure to timely take necessary actions," so the same event is both automatically excused and conditionally excused. The threshold words "substantial and extraordinary" also supply no measurable boundary.

The Indemnifying Party is "the Party from which another person seeks or is entitled to indemnification," so mere assertion by any person makes a Party an Indemnifying Party. That is broader than Article 9, which imposes indemnity only between the two Parties.

KPIs are defined only as "any of the rating factors used to measure performance," with the actual indicators left to Exhibit E, which Section 4.13.1 admits the Parties are still "in the process of completing." The performance measures against which breach is judged are therefore not fixed by the instrument.

An MBI Network Extension must be "funded in whole or in part by MTC," yet Section 3.6.1.2(a) lets Network Operator claim credit for its own funds expended to construct "MBI Network Extensions" and Section 4.5.7 gives MTC ownership "regardless of the source of its funding." The funding element of the definition cannot be squared with those sections.

The MTC Network is defined to include "any MBI Network Extensions and IRUs," while Section 4.5.5 makes Network Operator Network Extensions the operator's sole property and Section 2.39 says an extension becomes part of the MTC Network unless the operator proves otherwise. The perimeter of the asset the operator must maintain is contestable.

The second sentence is circular: an extension "shall become part of the MTC Network unless it is a Network Extension and the Network Operator establishes to MTC's reasonable satisfaction that it is not or does not become part of the MTC Network." The test defines the result by reference to itself and gives no criteria.

A Network Operator Network Extension must be "funded and owned by the Network Operator" yet "excludes any Network Extension funded by MTC unless otherwise agreed," leaving jointly funded extensions unallocated. Section 4.5.7's rule that MTC owns MBI extensions "regardless of the source of its funding" makes the overlap worse.

Deemed fees are measured by what a third party would pay "for similar services on the MTC Network," and "similar" is given no benchmark beyond a single illustrative example. The amount of phantom revenue on which revenue sharing is computed is therefore indeterminate.

After enumerating specific policies, the definition adds "any additional policies reasonably required by MTC to meet legal requirements," an open-ended catch-all that MTC may populate unilaterally while Section 4.12 demands "full compliance with all Network Policies." The enumerated list and the catch-all pull against each other.

The definition enumerates four revenue sources in (a)–(d) and then sweeps in "any amounts earned by Network Operator from services related to the MTC Network, other than the categories expressly excluded," so the enumerated list and the catch-all cannot both be given full effect. Whether a given receipt is Network Revenue, on which revenue sharing and the CAPEX and decommissioning payments turn, is open.

A Network Segment is whatever MTC defines during construction "and thereafter by mutual agreement," leaving no segment boundaries fixed if the parties do not agree. Section 3.6.1.5(b) prices the dark fiber option by "the highest number of strands leased in any Network Segment," so the undefined unit drives money.

An Officer's Certificate is said to have contents "binding upon the entity," a phrase that does not say whether it is a warranty, an estoppel, or merely evidence. Its effect where a certificate later proves inaccurate (Sections 3.6.1.2, 4.9.9.4) is unspecified.

Price Caps are said to be "the prices set forth in Exhibit F," but the Agreement's exhibit list assigns Price Caps to Exhibit D and makes Exhibit F the Master Services Agreement with EOPSS and ITD. The definition points to the wrong exhibit.

The carve-out says Network Operator Network Extension prices are in its "sole discretion" except that bandwidth charges to MassDOT, ITD or EOPSS are "governed by Section 4.7.2," but 4.7.2 caps those charges at 85% of the Price Schedule, which by this same definition does not apply to extensions. The two provisions cannot both be applied to an extension customer.

A Renewal Decision must conform to "the requirements of Section 3.2," but Section 3.2 states no requirements for any decision and the defined term appears nowhere else in the Agreement. The definition is unanchored.

Retail Service is defined solely by the identity of the provider — "services provided by a Third Party Service Provider" — which makes Section 4.8's prohibition on the Network Operator providing Retail Services impossible to breach as a matter of definition. The definition and the operative prohibition cannot both be given effect.

"Services" means "all performance obligations of the Network Operator hereunder," a wholly circular definition that Section 4.7.1 then extends to unwritten tasks "deemed to be implied." What is and is not a Service is not determinable from the term itself.

The SLA definition describes a document whose substance is left to Exhibit E, which Section 4.13.1 concedes is still being completed and is not attached. The service levels the definition presupposes do not exist in the instrument.

"Term" runs "until the expiration or termination of this Agreement," but Section 8.4.1 provides that neither the Term nor the operator's obligations "shall be deemed to have expired or terminated" until services transfer assistance is complete. Whether the Term ends on the date fixed by Section 3.1 or is extended indefinitely by 8.4.1 is unresolved.

The definition sweeps in "any organization other than Network Operator providing retail broadband service," which on its face includes an Affiliate of the Network Operator that Section 4.8 permits to be a Third Party Service Provider. The scope of the enumerated carrier categories versus the general opening words is contestable.

Clause (c) makes "lit transmission service of not less than 10 Gbps to an institutional customer" a Wholesale Service, which permits the Network Operator to serve an end user directly notwithstanding Section 4.8's prohibition on its providing Retail Services. The boundary between the two is unstable.

The Term "will terminate upon the tenth (10th) anniversary of the Commencement Date," yet Section 8.4.1 says the Term shall not be deemed expired or terminated until services transfer assistance is completed or waived by MTC. The two provisions give different end dates for the same Term.

Renewal is "by mutual agreement of the parties," yet Section 2.54 defines a "Renewal Decision" as a written MTC decision "conforming to the requirements of Section 3.2" — requirements this Section does not contain. What Section 3.2 requires of MTC in responding to a Renewal Request cannot be determined.

A Renewal Request may be made only "within the period from thirty (30) to thirty-two (32) months prior to the expiration" with time of the essence, and the section says nothing about the consequence of a request made outside that two-month window. Whether a late request is void or merely voidable is unaddressed.

Either Party may walk away from renewal negotiations after the 28-month date, but Sections 3.6.1.3 and 3.6.1.4 attach very different dark-fiber pricing consequences to which Party "notifies" the other that it does not wish to renew. Terminating negotiations under 3.4 without such a notification leaves the pricing branch unassigned.

The rights are granted only "upon expiration of the Term," although the heading of Section 3.6 is "Upon Termination or Expiration" and Section 3.6.2 addresses termination for cause; what happens on a termination that is neither expiration nor MTC-for-cause (e.g. under 8.6 or 8.3.1) is not stated. The trigger for the option is ambiguous.
The right is to lease "between four (4) and eight (8) strands" without saying who elects the number within that range or on what basis. The quantity term of the option is left indeterminate.

The net-operating-loss measuring period runs "until the last calendar quarter before the date of the Request for Renewal," but no term "Request for Renewal" is defined (Section 2.55 defines "Renewal Request") and Section 3.6.1.3(d) contemplates that no such request is ever made. In that case the calculation has no end date.

Clause (c) triggers this pricing table simply "upon the expiry of the Term of this Agreement," which occurs in every case, so this table would always apply and would displace the different, less favourable table Section 3.6.1.4 prescribes when the Network Operator declines to renew. The two sections cannot both be given effect.

This table applies where Network Operator declines renewal, but Section 3.6.1.3(c) makes its own table applicable "upon the expiry of the Term" in all events, and the two produce different exercise prices on the same facts. Which controls is not stated.

The adjustment refers to "the per strand rate stated in Section 3.6.1.3 or 3.1.6.4," and there is no Section 3.1.6.4 — the evident intended reference is 3.6.1.4. The mis-citation leaves the second pricing table arguably unadjusted for CPI.

This prices the option on "the highest number of strands leased in any Network Segment regardless of disclaimers of use made pursuant to Section 3.6.1.11," while 3.6.1.11 provides that disclaimed strands are excluded and all rights in them become void. Whether a disclaimer reduces what the operator pays cannot be answered consistently.

Payment is due "on or before the end of the Term," yet Section 3.6.1 makes the rights arise only "upon expiration of the Term" and conditions them on NTIA approval that may not yet exist. The operator is required to pay before it is known whether the option exists.

"Total discounts available under this Section shall not exceed $6,000,000" does not say whether "this Section" is 3.6.1.7, 3.6.1, or all of 3.6, nor whether the cap is per strand or in the aggregate, though the tables in 3.6.1.3 can generate dollar-for-dollar discounts far exceeding that figure. The cap's field of operation is ambiguous.

The 25-year lease commences "upon termination or expiration of the Term," although Section 3.6.1 grants the underlying right only upon expiration and Section 3.6.2 denies it upon termination for cause. The commencement trigger does not match the trigger for the right itself.

New extensions and connections must comply with "MTC's policies then applicable to others" and fees "at then-prevailing prices," neither of which is fixed or constrained by any standard of reasonableness. The post-term cost of the leased fiber is left to MTC's later policy-making.

The maintenance baseline is "half the actual maintenance costs ... during the last two full calendar year prior to the exercise," which is grammatically broken and does not say whether the figure is the average of the two years or their total. The pro rata formula that follows is applied to a baseline that cannot be computed with confidence.

Disclaimed strands are excluded from the operator's pro rata cost shares here, but Section 3.6.1.5(b) fixes the total exercise price on the highest strand count "regardless of disclaimers of use made pursuant to Section 3.6.1.11." The effect of a disclaimer differs between the two provisions.

It is unclear whether the trailing condition "and the Network Operator has invested less than $3,000,000" qualifies only clause (b) or both clauses (a) and (b), which decides whether a for-cause termination alone defeats the Dark Fiber Rights. The syntax of the compound condition is genuinely ambiguous.

Network Operator is made "responsible for all aspects" of the network and the enumerated duties are stated to be its responsibilities "generally," so the specific list in 4.1.1–4.1.9 sits against an unbounded general obligation. Whether an unlisted cost or task falls within the operator's duties is left open.

Section 4.1.10.1 requires a draft of the capitalized "Initial Plan" pursuant to Section 4.9.3.1, but no "Initial Plan" is defined in Article 2 and 4.9.3.1 speaks only of an "initial plan." The deliverable's required content is fixed only by the loose narrative description in 4.9.3.1.

Deadlines are to be "reasonably adjusted" for MTC-caused information delays, with no mechanism, no measure and no decision-maker specified. Whether an adjustment has occurred, and by how much, is left at large.

MTC is "solely responsible for design, engineering, installation and construction decisions," yet Section 4.9.2.9 has MTC agree only to "seek advice" and take "commercially reasonable steps" so the network is built to let the operator meet the Agreement's parameters. Where a design defect prevents SLA performance, the allocation of responsibility between these two sections is contestable.
